tasks.title: `--inbox` then `--wait` re-delivers turns already read (two cursors disagree)
tasks.note: `--inbox` is non-destructive and `--say` never moves the cursor; composed, an `--inbox` followed by `--wait` re-delivers everything just shown. Fix is an explicit `--mark-read`, not consuming by default. See ADR-013 (roadmap v2/v3 boundary). UPDATE session 16 (2026-09-24), from Atlas (SIA planner, SIA record session 90, under D-039/D-003), on v1.8.0 (local hub-talk 003f57d + tcm hub): room k57frxw0ptb8tadmqdwy0khhks8ey006, ~02:35Z, `--as atlas --inbox` printed 16 turns, ending "16 turns, 2 unread after turn 13 (cursor unchanged)"; /reads then showed atlas lastRead 16 via inbox; the next `--wait --wait-timeout 3600` returned at once with exit 0 and re-printed turns 15 and 16. There was no new turn; grok's real reply came later as turn 18. This is DESIGNED behaviour at ea9d057: scripts/hub-talk.mjs:328-391 keeps two cursors. The hub read mark means 'delivered' and --inbox advances it; the local cursor means 'handed over by --wait' and only --wait advances it. Two consequences, and they falsify the earlier 'noise only, never blocked anything': (1) a seat that reads 'wait returned, exit 0' as 'new reply' acts on a reply it has already handled (Atlas caught it only by reading the output); (2) since v1.8.0 the two marks visibly disagree, so /reads says read through 16 while --wait re-delivers 15-16, an ADR-013 ambiguous-silence shape. Atlas's expectation, labelled as Atlas's own view and not a ruling: --wait starts from the mark --inbox just set, or --inbox advances the wait cursor. Raised P2->P1. tasks.title: Read receipts: a sender can see a turn is unread by participant X, and since when
tasks.note: SIA requirement R-a (SIA T-160, evidence at SIA 4e334d8). On 2026-09-23 Atlas sent turns 6 and 7 into room k579hndqdr1mxnahy0px1dy8ks8eyef3; Grok 4.7 in Cursor, holding SIA's developer seat, was idle and never read them. The send receipts were true and said nothing about reading, so neither side could tell; Aaron found it by looking at the Cursor window. Today the only read cursor is client-side (scripts/hub-cursor.mjs, a local file written only by --wait); the server holds no read state, checked at f7f102d. Requirement: visible to the sender with no client-side change needed to see it. ADR-013's class: silence that cannot tell 'no messages' from 'no listener'. WHAT MARKS A TURN READ (SIA's requirement, from Atlas as customer, 2026-09-23): read means delivered into the AGENT'S context, not fetched by a process. A background listener or daemon that consumes turns for a seat whose model never sees them would make receipts lie in exactly the Grok case. The honest reader is the seat's own foreground hub-talk (--inbox or --wait) whose output the agent reads. If a design cannot tell these apart, the row states it as a named limit. How it is met is this repo's call. IDENTITY LIMIT, accepted by SIA as customer (Atlas, 2026-09-23): under the shared dev-key any seat can mark turns read as any participant, so 'unread by X' means unread by whoever uses the name X. SIA accepts this for local trusted seats until T-003, because it needs to tell silence from absence, not to authenticate. This is SIA's acceptance with its limit, not a property of the feature. Live use needs a tcm redeploy (D-003 coordination).

tasks.title: Wake an idle IDE seat that has an unread turn in its room
tasks.note: SIA requirement R-b (SIA T-160). An idle IDE seat either cannot go idle while its room holds an unread turn, or is woken with it. A Cursor agent sees hub messages only when it runs hub-talk itself. Joint acceptance with T-049 (SIA's words): a turn sent to an idle Cursor seat is either acted on without Aaron touching that window, or the sender is told it is unread by that seat, with the time. Depends on server-side read state (T-049) to know what is unread. FIRST UNKNOWN, ANSWERED FROM DOCUMENTATION ONLY (Relay, session 15, cursor.com/docs/agent/hooks read 2026-09-23; not tested on the installed Cursor, whose version is unrecorded): Cursor has a `stop` hook, called when the agent loop ends, input {status: completed|aborted|error, loop_count}. It may return {followup_message}, which Cursor auto-submits as the next USER message, so the turn lands in the agent's context (T-049's definition of read). Per-script `loop_limit` defaults to 5 auto follow-ups per conversation (null removes the cap); `timeout` is per-script in seconds with an unstated platform default; `failClosed` exists. Config in <project>/.cursor/hooks.json (checked in) or ~/.cursor/hooks.json; for followup_message the last response wins across sources. `stop` also runs in Cursor cloud agents. What this gives: a wake AT THE MOMENT THE AGENT STOPS, not after. The hook can check for unread turns, or block on a long-poll up to its timeout, and feed a turn back. What it does not give: once the hook returns empty, the seat is idle and nothing in Cursor wakes it for a turn that arrives later. The requirement's first branch ('cannot go idle') holds only for as long as the hook blocks; past that the second branch (sender told unread-since-T, T-049) carries the acceptance. LOOP CAP (SIA's requirement, Atlas as customer, 2026-09-23): the default 5 follow-ups is below SIA's real traffic (7 planner turns in one room on 2026-09-23; a full candidate round runs more), and past the cap the next wake silently does not happen. Whatever ships must either set loop_limit deliberately, stating the value and why, or make reaching the cap visible to the sender (T-049's unread-since-T is that route). Unknowns still open: the default and maximum timeout; whether followup_message is honoured when status is aborted (the user pressed stop; it should not be); whether the Grok Bot surface runs hooks at all. These need a live trial in a Cursor window, which is Aaron's machine and falls under the SIA pause. LIVE EVIDENCE (session 17, docs/case-studies/2026-09-25-grokbot-marketplace-watcher.md, gap G3): in the melve-76<->grokbot room neither side woke on hub traffic; read receipts showed grokbot stalled at turn 11 until Aaron nudged it in its own chat, and a Claude Code background --wait was blocked by the auto-mode classifier. Candidate patterns named there: a routine polling --inbox on the Grok Bot side, a permission allow-rule for hub-talk --wait on the Claude Code side, or a push bridge (hub to Telegram or a CC channel). — SESSION 20 (D-029): folded into Loop 8b (T-076). Its acceptance is carried there; close with T-076.
